content: Influenza virus infection among children, defined as individuals under 18 years of age, has been a nationally reportable condition. During the 2004–2005 influenza season, the annual number of seasonal influenza-associated deaths among children reported to the CDC ranged from 47 in 2004–2005 to 88 in 2007–2008. However, during the 2009 H1N1 influenza pandemic (April 2009–March 2010), over 300 deaths in children attributable to laboratory-confirmed H1N1 influenza were reported to the CDC in the United States, with the majority of these children having one or more underlying medical conditions. It is estimated that over 1,000 deaths occurred during this period. Deaths among children attributed to co-infection with influenza and Staphylococcus aureus, particularly methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA), have increased. The severity of illness in cases of co-infection is greater compared to influenza infection alone. The reason for this increase in co-infections is not fully understood but may reflect a rising prevalence of MRSA colonization in the general population, with some strains carrying specific virulence factors. Among healthy younger adults, illness caused by seasonal influenza is typically not severe and rarely results in hospitalization, especially when compared to children under 5 years, adults aged 65 years or older, pregnant women, or individuals with chronic medical conditions. However, influenza illness among healthy adults aged 19–49 years is a significant cause of outpatient medical visits and work absenteeism. The impact of influenza varies considerably by season, making it challenging to estimate attack rates in healthy younger adults. On average, five workdays are lost per illness episode, with approximately 4 million outpatient visits, 32,000 hospitalizations, and 680 deaths annually attributed to influenza. Hospitalization rates during typical influenza seasons are significantly higher for individuals aged 65 years or older compared to younger age groups. Among adults aged 65 years or older with underlying medical conditions, the rate of influenza-associated hospitalizations is approximately 560 per 100,000 persons, compared to 190 per 100,000 among healthy individuals in the same age group. Adults aged 50–64 years with underlying medical conditions also face a substantially increased risk of hospitalization during influenza seasons compared to their healthy counterparts. Influenza is a major contributor to the annual increase in deaths attributed to pneumonia and influenza observed during the winter months. Between 1976 and 2001, an estimated annual average of 32,651 influenza-related deaths occurred among adults aged 65 years or older, with the highest risk of death observed in the oldest age groups. Adults aged 85 years or older were 16 times more likely to die from influenza-related illness compared to those aged 65–69 years. During the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, adults under 65 years of age were at higher risk for influenza-related complications, particularly those aged 50–64 years with underlying medical conditions, compared to typical influenza seasons. The distribution of hospitalizations by age group during the 2009–2010 pandemic differed from usual seasonal influenza patterns, with more hospitalizations among younger age groups and fewer among adults aged 65 years or older. Hospitalization rates during this period exceeded those seen in any recent influenza season among adults aged 65 years or younger. Pneumonia with evidence of invasive bacterial co-infection was reported in approximately one-third of fatal cases in autopsy studies. In critically ill adults requiring mechanical ventilation, Streptococcus pneumoniae pneumonia at admission was identified as an independent risk factor for death. Obesity, defined as a body mass index (BMI) of 30 or higher, and particularly morbid obesity (BMI ≥ 40), appeared to be risk factors for hospitalization and death in some studies during the 2009 H1N1 pandemic. Additional research is needed to determine whether obesity is a specific risk factor for complications caused by 2009 H1N1-like influenza viruses or a previously unrecognized risk factor for influenza-related complications caused by other influenza viruses. The 2009 H1N1 pandemic also highlighted racial and ethnic disparities in the risk for influenza-related complications among adults. Higher hospitalization rates were observed among Black individuals, and a disproportionate number of deaths occurred among American Indians/Alaska Natives and indigenous populations in other countries. These disparities may be partially attributable to a higher prevalence of underlying medical conditions or inequities in access to medical care among these racial and ethnic groups. The duration of influenza symptoms is prolonged, and the severity of illness is increased among individuals with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. A retrospective study of women aged 15–64 years enrolled in Tennessee's Medicaid program found that the attributable risk for cardiopulmonary hospitalizations among women with HIV infection was higher during influenza seasons than before or after influenza circulation. The risk for hospitalization was higher for HIV-infected women compared to women with other underlying medical conditions. Influenza is also associated with an increased risk of death in the general population. Among individuals aged 25–54 years, the mortality rate is approximately 10 deaths per 100,000 persons, while for those aged 65 years or older, the rate is 64–70 deaths per 100,000 persons.
